items.article_search_text: Oscar Piastri explains how a red flag disrupted his run and led to an unexpected early exit from qualifying. Piastri rejects red-flag excuse. Tyres, not timing, decided his fate. McLaren now has a Q2 puzzle to solve. Oscar Piastri says a late red flag did not cause his unexpected qualifying exit at Interlagos. The McLaren driver finished 12th in a rain-hit session, missing the top ten by just over two tenths. His team-mate Lando Norris claimed pole with a 1m 27.470s lap, while Piastri’s best effort was 1m 30.369s. A switch from wet tyres to intermediates reshaped the battle, and Piastri believes the timing of that call mattered more than the session interruption. How the red flag affected Piastri’s qualifying exit With around 45 seconds left in Q2, Rafael Camara crashed his Haas at the final major braking zone. Race control stopped the session, denying several drivers—including Piastri—a final chance to improve. The interruption was real, but it affected the whole field rather than singling out the Australian. “Everyone would have got another lap,” Piastri said, rejecting the idea that the red flag alone explained his early exit. He acknowledged that the extra run might have helped, but pointed instead to the need to have the right tyre ready at the right moment. That distinction matters: the session interruption cut short his opportunity, but did not create the underlying grip problem. The result leaves a sharp contrast inside McLaren: Norris converted the changing conditions into pole, while Piastri could not find enough time on the intermediate tyres. The Australian’s wider season story has centred on his place in the team, including this report on his commitment to McLaren. At Interlagos, though, the immediate question was execution over a handful of laps. Tyre timing and track conditions explain the gap Piastri admitted that the team may have waited too long before moving to intermediates. He had just completed a lap, but the tyres needed another run or two to build temperature; lines that worked on the full wets no longer suited the changing surface. In mixed conditions, grip can shift faster than a driver can adapt, and the clock offers little room to recover. https://www.youtube.com/watch?vZUrgCph5IRk That left the 1m 30.369s lap short of what Q3 demanded. Piastri said there was “a lot more time” available, and suggested that another lap and better decisions could have put him through. For Formula 1 teams, the decision is not simply wet versus intermediate; it is when the tyre can deliver temperature without sacrificing a final timed attempt. There is useful context in the team-mate comparison. Norris’s 1m 27.470s pole showed how much pace the McLaren could produce, but it does not erase the changing track conditions across the session. For more on the pair’s competition, see Norris under pressure as Piastri impresses; this qualifying split was decided by timing and tyre preparation, not a simple lack of car speed. What Piastri’s early exit means for the São Paulo race Despite the disappointing grid position, Piastri said he felt comfortable with the car in the dry and that the team had a solid baseline. A dry race would give him a more predictable platform, while further rain could reopen the same tyre-temperature challenge that shaped qualifying. Either way, the race weekend is not defined by one interrupted session. https://www.youtube.com/watch?vMIAo6VJ9onQ The focus now shifts to converting that dry-weather confidence into forward progress from 12th. Piastri has not blamed luck, and his account points to a specific review for McLaren: whether the move to intermediates came late and whether the out-lap plan gave them enough time to work. The red flag closed the door on one more attempt; tyre choice had already narrowed the route to Q3. As a sports journalist trained on the trackside and by the pitch, I live to the rhythm of race weekends and match nights. I love numbers and strategies, but above all, the human stories behind performance. At home in the paddocks as much as in amateur clubs, I stand for sports that are accessible to everyone. I write with the rigor of an analyst and the passion of a fan who never misses a session.

items.article_search_text: ‘Mate, you told me to back off! What the hell?’ 7NEWS brings you the latest local news from Australia and around the world. Stay up to date with all of the breaking sport, politics, entertainment, finance, weather and business headlines. Today's news, live updates & all the latest breaking stories from 7NEWS. Australian Formula One star Oscar Piastri will start from 10th on the gird for the Sao Paulo grand prix after Lando Norris put his McLaren on pole position for the third year in a row. It was a wild Saturday (Sunday AEDT) at Interlagos in tough ‌conditions after a long delay caused by torrential rain, and extra mechanical considerations for many drivers. George Russell qualified second fastest for Mercedes, 0.204 slower, but dropped down the ‌grid due to a five-place penalty, with his newly-crowned world champion teammate Kimi Antonelli replacing him alongside last year’s race winner and champion. Ferrari’s ‌Charles Leclerc was fourth fastest but has a 10-place grid drop due to power unit changes, which meant Racing Bulls’ Liam Lawson will start third and Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg fourth. “The big shock there is Oscar Piastri,” Sky Sports commentator David Croft said. “He won’t be continuing in this qualifying session”. With the rain getting heavier and leaving no chance for anyone to improve on their times in the final phase, the clock ticked down for the last five minutes without a car on track. “Today is about getting on ‌pole. It doesn’t ‌really matter how you ⁠do it, so very pleased with that,” Norris said after a qualifying that started ​and was then halted for nearly an hour and a half. Russell was furious not to be fastest, wanting to make a statement despite knowing he had a penalty but having to abort his quick lap when he came up behind Williams’ Alex Albon. “Mate, you told me to back off! What the hell?,” he shouted over team radio after realising his day was done. “P2. I don’t ⁠want to be P2. I want to be P1.” Red Bull’s four-time champion ​Max Verstappen, with a 30 place grid penalty due to power unit changes, sat out the second phase that was red-flagged when Haas debutant Rafael Camara crashed. Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, who will also be starting at the back of the grid ​due ​to engine penalties amounting to an impossible 65 place ​drop, also went out. There was then a further delay to clear ‌debris before the decisive third phase. Conditions had eased in Q2, with double world champion Fernando Alonso leaning on his experience and the first to switch to intermediates. Camara earlier had the home crowd roaring when he reached the second phase but fellow-Brazilian Gabriel Bortoleto had a nightmare for the second year running when he went off and qualified last. Bortoleto slid into the tyre wall with seven minutes to go ​but returned to the track and made his way back to the pits where the damage proved too extensive to ​fix in the time available. Both Alpines ⁠also went out at the first hurdle along with the two Cadillacs and Aston Martin’s ​Lance Stroll. Journalist from Australian news agency, Australian Associated Press.
